topicName: I/O Streams vs NIO Channels, Buffers, and Selectors
content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Mastering I/O Streams vs NIO Channels, Buffers, and Selectors in Java"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Java provides two distinct architectures for handling input and output operations: the legacy java.io package (I/O Streams) and the modern java.nio package (New I/O). Understanding when and how to use Streams versus Channels, Buffers, and Selectors is essential for writing high-performance, scalable network and file processing applications."},{"order":3,"type":"heading","text":"1. Traditional I/O Streams (java.io)"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Traditional I/O is stream-oriented. This means Java reads or writes one or more bytes at a time from a stream. The core characteristics of I/O Streams include:"},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Blocking I/O: When a thread invokes a read() or write() method, it blocks until data is read or written completely. The thread cannot do anything else during this time."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Stream-oriented: Data is processed sequentially without caching, making it difficult to move back and forth in the data stream without buffering wrappers."},{"order":7,"type":"code","text":"try (InputStream in = new FileInputStream(\"source.txt\"); OutputStream out = new FileOutputStream(\"dest.txt\")) { int byteData; while ((byteData = in.read()) != -1) { out.write(byteData); } }"},{"order":8,"type":"heading","text":"2. Java NIO: Channels, Buffers, and Selectors"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"Introduced in Java 1.4, Java NIO (New I/O) provides block-oriented, non-blocking I/O capabilities. It revolves around three core components: Channels, Buffers, and Selectors."},{"order":10,"type":"subheading","text":"Buffers"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"In NIO, data is read into a Buffer first, rather than reading it directly from a stream. A Buffer is essentially a block of memory you can write to and read from. It maintains internal tracking markers like capacity, position, and limit."},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"Channels"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Channels are similar to streams, but with key differences. Channels are bi-directional (can read and write), and they operate in conjunction with Buffers. Data is always read from a channel into a buffer, or written from a buffer into a channel."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"try (RandomAccessFile file = new RandomAccessFile(\"data.txt\", \"rw\"); FileChannel channel = file.getChannel()) { ByteBuffer buffer = ByteBuffer.allocate(48); int bytesRead = channel.read(buffer); while (bytesRead != -1) { buffer.flip(); while (buffer.hasRemaining()) { System.out.print((char) buffer.get()); } buffer.clear(); bytesRead = channel.read(buffer); } }"},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"Selectors"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"A Selector allows a single thread to monitor multiple channels (such as network connections). By registering channels with a Selector, you can examine which channels have data ready for reading, writing, or connection. This is the foundation of scalable non-blocking network servers."},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"Selector selector = Selector.open(); ServerSocketChannel serverChannel = ServerSocketChannel.open(); serverChannel.configureBlocking(false); serverChannel.bind(new InetSocketAddress(8080)); serverChannel.register(selector, SelectionKey.OP_ACCEPT);"},{"order":18,"type":"heading","text":"3. Summary Comparison"},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"I/O Streams: Stream-oriented, Blocking, Simple to implement, Ideal for low-volume or simple file operations."},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"NIO Channels & Buffers: Block-oriented, Can be non-blocking, Highly efficient, Ideal for high-throughput file transfers."},{"order":21,"type":"bullet_point","text":"NIO Selectors: Enables multiplexed, non-blocking network architecture, Essential for high-concurrency servers (e.g., chat apps, web servers)."}]
